title: How heavy can a dead star be?
blurb: A young physicist from Madras, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, worked out that a white dwarf star cannot be more than about 1.4 times as heavy as the Sun.

original.title: The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs

cards.b: When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel at its centre, it collapses. It squeezes into a small, very dense star called a white dwarf. A white dwarf holds itself up with a push from its tightly packed electrons. But can that push hold up any star, however heavy it is?

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was born in Lahore in 1910 and grew up in Madras, now Chennai. He studied physics at Presidency College in Madras. In 1930 he went to the University of Cambridge in England. In 1931, while still in his early twenties, he published papers on white dwarf stars.

img.alt: A drawing of NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory in space, which was named after Chandrasekhar

cards.b: Chandrasekhar did not need a telescope for this. He used maths. He combined two big ideas of physics. One is relativity, which explains very fast things. The other is quantum mechanics, which explains very tiny things. With them he worked out what happens to the electrons' push inside a white dwarf as the star gets heavier.

The electrons' push can only do so much. Suppose a white dwarf is heavier than about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun. Then the push cannot hold it up, and it collapses. This is now called the Chandrasekhar limit. It means that stars much heavier than the Sun cannot end as white dwarfs. They must explode or become black holes.

Today the limit is basic to much of astronomy. But at first it was argued over. In January 1935, the famous astronomer Arthur Eddington clashed with Chandrasekhar about it. Some questions are still open. Astronomers believe a white dwarf pushed over the limit blows up, but what pushes it over is still a mystery.

When a white dwarf blows up, it makes a Type Ia supernova. These explosions shine with a brightness astronomers can predict, so they use them to measure how the universe is growing. That led to the discovery of dark energy. In 1983 Chandrasekhar shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on how stars are built and change.

img.alt: The glowing remains of a Type Ia supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, photographed by Hubble
img.credit: NASA, ESA (Hubble Space Telescope), public domain

cards.b: Feel packed things push back. Revathi fills a steel tumbler loosely with cotton wool and presses it down with her palm. At first it squashes easily. As it packs tighter, it pushes back harder. A white dwarf is packed so tightly that its electrons push back. Above about 1.4 Suns, even that push is not enough.

Chandrasekhar was in his twenties when a famous older scientist argued against his idea. Today his limit is used everywhere in astronomy. When an expert disagrees with you, how do you decide whether to change your mind or keep going? What would help you check?
